metadata.summary: This article updates FIGO AUB System 1, which defines normal menstrual parameters and symptoms of abnormal uterine bleeding, and FIGO AUB System 2, which classifies potential causes using PALM-COEIN. It clarifies diagnostic categories and leiomyoma subclassification and outlines a clinical investigation approach for nongestational abnormal uterine bleeding during the reproductive years. The systems are intended to support consistent clinical care, education, and research.

target_population: Women of reproductive age with nongestational abnormal uterine bleeding
Women in the peri-menopause with abnormal uterine bleeding

recognition: AUB associated with systemic pharmacotherapy or an intrauterine system or device is classified as AUB-I.
The document describes AUB associated with drugs that interfere with ovulation and with anticoagulants. It states that rivaroxaban appears to affect menstrual bleeding volume more than warfarin.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Chlamydial infection of the endometrium and chronic endometritis
infection_management.management: The document suggests considering testing symptomatic patients for chlamydial infection. Cervical testing may be reasonable, although its correspondence with endometrial infection is uncertain. If chronic endometritis is identified, classify the patient as AUB-E.

therapies_index.name: hysteroscopically directed polypectomy
therapies_index.administration: The document notes that removal of a suspected polyp may be performed during office hysteroscopy.

therapies_index.name: estrogens
key_toxicities: Their use is among the pharmacologic exposures the document associates with iatrogenic AUB.

therapies_index.name: progestins
key_toxicities: Their use is among the pharmacologic exposures the document associates with iatrogenic AUB.

therapies_index.name: androgens
key_toxicities: Their use is among the pharmacologic exposures the document associates with iatrogenic AUB.

therapies_index.name: phenothiazines
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies these as agents that affect dopamine metabolism.
key_toxicities: They are cited among nonsteroidal pharmaceuticals that can contribute to ovulatory disorders and associated AUB.

therapies_index.name: tricyclic antidepressants
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies these as agents that affect dopamine metabolism.
key_toxicities: They are cited among nonsteroidal pharmaceuticals that can contribute to ovulatory disorders and associated AUB.

therapies_index.name: rivaroxaban
key_toxicities: It appears to have a greater impact on menstrual bleeding volume than traditional vitamin K antagonists exemplified by warfarin.

therapies_index.name: warfarin
key_toxicities: The document associates anticoagulant use with AUB and uses warfarin as an example of a traditional vitamin K antagonist.

therapies_index.name: intrauterine systems or devices
key_toxicities: The document classifies AUB associated with their use as iatrogenic.

special_populations.considerations: Vaginal access may make TVUS, contrast sonohysterography, and office hysteroscopy impracticable. MRI has a role; hysteroscopy with indicated biopsies under appropriate anesthesia may be the best approach. Menstrual bleeding patterns may also differ during adolescence.
Menstrual bleeding patterns may change near the end of the reproductive years.

special_populations.population: Women with risk factors for endometrial neoplasia
special_populations.considerations: Most cited studies suggest considering endometrial sampling above an age threshold, usually 45 years. Obesity substantially increases the risk of premalignant and malignant endometrial changes, including among women in the third and fourth decades of life. Women with Lynch Syndrome have a lifetime endometrial cancer risk of up to 60%, with a mean age at diagnosis of 48–50 years. These factors inform selection for endometrial sampling; sampling is also necessary, if possible, when AUB persists and remains unexplained or inadequately treated.

If imaging is unavailable, the minimum description of leiomyomas should include a clinical estimate of uterine size expressed as equivalent to a gravid uterus of “X” weeks. Routine MRI assessment is not mandatory, given its limited availability in many healthcare systems, but MRI may be used when necessary and available.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with pre-existing AUB-related anemia
special_populations.considerations: The document associates pre-existing AUB-related anemia with increased maternal morbidity and mortality. The FIGO AUB systems themselves apply only to nongestational bleeding.

recommendations.statement: Use the revised FIGO terminology for AUB symptoms rather than terms such as menorrhagia, metrorrhagia, oligomenorrhea, and dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
recommendations.context: Terminology for bleeding during the reproductive years.
recommendations.rationale: The older terms were inconsistently defined and used.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.1 | Revision of terminologies and definitions of symptoms of abnormal uterine bleeding

recommendations.statement: For clinical use, define HMB by menstrual blood loss that disrupts physical, social, emotional, and/or material quality of life; treat HMB as a symptom rather than a diagnosis.
recommendations.context: FIGO AUB System 1 adopts the clinical definition attributed to the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.1 | Revision of terminologies and definitions of symptoms of abnormal uterine bleeding

recommendations.statement: Apply the age-specific normal limits for shortest-to-longest cycle variation: 18–25 years ≤9 days; 26–41 years ≤7 days; and 42–45 years ≤9 days. For practical purposes, normal cycle-length variation may instead be expressed as ±4 days.
recommendations.context: FIGO AUB System 1 definition of menstrual regularity.
recommendations.rationale: The revised limits exclude occasional unusually long or short cycles from the definition of irregular bleeding.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.1 | Revision of terminologies and definitions of symptoms of abnormal uterine bleeding

recommendations.statement: For diagnosis of adenomyosis within FIGO AUB System 2, use of the transvaginal ultrasonography-based MUSA criteria is suggested.
recommendations.context: An imaging-based FIGO subclassification system for adenomyosis was still being developed.
recommendations.rationale: There was no consensus on how many or which sonographic findings establish the diagnosis with reasonable certainty.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: Distinguish Type 0 from Type 1 and Type 6 from Type 7 leiomyomas by comparing stalk diameter with mean leiomyoma diameter; Types 0 and 7 have a stalk diameter of 10% or less than the mean leiomyoma diameter.
recommendations.context: FIGO leiomyoma subclassification.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: Use hysteroscopy at the lowest filling pressure that permits visualization of the endometrial cavity to distinguish Type 2 from Type 3 leiomyomas.
recommendations.context: FIGO leiomyoma subclassification.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: Distinguish Type 4 from Type 5 leiomyomas by assessing for distortion of the serosa with ultrasonography or MRI; serosal distortion indicates Type 5.
recommendations.context: FIGO leiomyoma subclassification.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: When describing leiomyomas, record at minimum an imaging-based estimate of total uterine volume and an estimate of the leiomyoma count as 1, 2, 3, 4, or greater than 4. If imaging is unavailable, record the uterine size estimated on examination as equivalent to a gravid uterus of “X” weeks.
recommendations.context: Minimum data set for investigators using FIGO leiomyoma subclassification.
recommendations.rationale: The examination-based alternative accommodates settings without imaging access.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: When transvaginal ultrasonography or MRI is available, document the position and estimated volume of up to four individual leiomyomas, including whether each lies in the upper half, lower half, or both. If there are more than four, record at least the volume of the largest and also record volumes of other lesions judged equally or more relevant to clinical decisions. If the endometrium is visible, describe each documented leiomyoma’s relationship to it using FIGO classification.
recommendations.context: Additional FIGO leiomyoma documentation guidance; positional descriptors are anterior, posterior, left, right, or center.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: Consider using the FIGO diagnostic matrix to evaluate reproductive-aged patients with AUB and document which potential causes have been assessed.
recommendations.context: FIGO AUB System 2 evaluation.
recommendations.rationale: The matrix records both findings and the status of investigations.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)

recommendations.statement: First characterize bleeding symptoms with FIGO AUB System 1, then evaluate the potential causes in FIGO AUB System 2 as comprehensively as is practicable for the clinical circumstances and available resources; interpret whether each finding plausibly contributes to the symptoms.
recommendations.context: Clinical investigation during the reproductive years.
recommendations.rationale: A patient may have multiple findings, including structural lesions that are unlikely to explain the reported bleeding.
recommendations.source_heading: 6 | RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CLINICAL INVESTIGATION

recommendations.statement: In a reproductive-aged woman with suspected acute or chronic AUB, establish that bleeding is unrelated to pregnancy and originates from the cervical canal rather than another genital or adjacent site. A urine or serum assay for the β-subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) can confirm pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Initial assessment of genital tract bleeding.
recommendations.rationale: The FIGO AUB systems concern nongestational uterine bleeding, not bleeding from other sites.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.1 | General assessment

recommendations.statement: Evaluate women with acute or chronic AUB for iron deficiency, using serum ferritin if possible, and for associated anemia by measuring hemoglobin and/or hematocrit, preferably through a full blood count that includes platelets.
recommendations.context: General assessment after suspected or confirmed AUB.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.1 | General assessment

recommendations.statement: Once a cervical-canal or endometrial-cavity source is confirmed or suspected, systematically assess each component of the PALM-COEIN classification.
recommendations.context: FIGO AUB System 2 clinical evaluation.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.1 | General assessment

recommendations.statement: When ovulatory status is uncertain, measurement of serum progesterone timed to the best estimate of the mid-luteal phase may help confirm ovulation in the current cycle.
recommendations.context: Assessment of suspected ovulatory dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.2 | Determination of ovulatory status

recommendations.statement: Do not use endometrial biopsy to determine ovulatory status. If biopsy is appropriately performed to assess premalignant or malignant endometrial change, secretory histology may confirm that ovulation occurred.
recommendations.context: Determination of ovulatory status.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.2 | Determination of ovulatory status

recommendations.statement: Use a structured bleeding history as the initial screen for an underlying hemostatic disorder in women with excessive menstrual bleeding. The described screen is positive with HMB since menarche; one history of postpartum hemorrhage, surgery-related bleeding, or bleeding with dental work; or two or more of bruising 1–2 times per month, epistaxis 1–2 times per month, frequent gum bleeding, and a family history of bleeding symptoms.
recommendations.context: Screening instrument for coagulopathies in women with HMB.
recommendations.rationale: The structured history instrument is reported to have 90% sensitivity for detecting coagulopathy in women with HMB.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.3 | Screening for systemic disorders of hemostasis

recommendations.statement: After a positive coagulopathy screen, pursue further evaluation, often with consultation from a clinician specializing in coagulation disorders; testing may include von Willebrand factor, Ristocetin cofactor, partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and other measures.
recommendations.context: Follow-up of a positive structured bleeding-history screen.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.3 | Screening for systemic disorders of hemostasis

recommendations.statement: Select patients for endometrial sampling according to their combined risk of premalignant or malignant endometrial change, considering age, personal and genetic risk factors, and TVUS assessment of endometrial echocomplex thickness; sampling is not required for every patient with AUB.
recommendations.context: Endometrial evaluation in AUB.
recommendations.rationale: Risk differs across patients, including those with obesity or Lynch Syndrome.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.4 | Evaluation of the endometrium

recommendations.statement: Most cited studies suggest considering endometrial sampling for all women above a certain age, usually 45 years.
recommendations.context: Age-based selection for endometrial biopsy; the document notes that some studies do not find age independently important.
recommendations.rationale: Most of the cited studies favor consideration of sampling above an age threshold.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.4 | Evaluation of the endometrium

recommendations.statement: When AUB persists and remains unexplained or inadequately treated, obtain endometrial sampling if possible, together with hysteroscopic assessment of the uterine cavity.
recommendations.context: Persistent AUB, irrespective of the clinical guideline used.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.4 | Evaluation of the endometrium

recommendations.statement: Obtain an adequate endometrial sample before regarding a patient as being at low risk for a malignant neoplasm.
recommendations.context: Interpretation of endometrial sampling.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.4 | Evaluation of the endometrium

recommendations.statement: Consider testing symptomatic patients for chlamydial infection of the endometrium, while recognizing that the relationship between cervical test results and endometrial infection is unclear.
recommendations.context: Assessment for an infectious contribution to AUB.
recommendations.rationale: The document describes a relationship between endometrial chlamydial infection and AUB.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.4 | Evaluation of the endometrium

recommendations.statement: Perform TVUS early in the investigation in most instances to screen for structural abnormalities affecting the endometrial cavity.
recommendations.context: Assessment for lesions including endometrial or endocervical polyps and submucous leiomyomas.
recommendations.rationale: TVUS is an important screening method, although a normal examination does not exclude every small lesion.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.5 | Evaluation of the structure of the endometrial cavity

recommendations.statement: If ultrasonography suggests an endometrial polyp or a leiomyoma approaching the cavity, or if image quality is inadequate, use a more sensitive assessment, generally hysteroscopy and/or contrast sonohysterography.
recommendations.context: Further evaluation after an abnormal or suboptimal initial cavity examination.
recommendations.rationale: Polyps and other small lesions can be missed on TVUS; the choice of subsequent technique depends on available resources.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.5 | Evaluation of the structure of the endometrial cavity

recommendations.statement: When vaginal access prevents TVUS, contrast sonohysterography, or office hysteroscopy, MRI has a role; hysteroscopy with indicated biopsies under appropriate anesthesia may be the best approach.
recommendations.context: Vaginal access may be difficult or impossible, particularly in adolescents and virginal women.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.5 | Evaluation of the structure of the endometrial cavity

recommendations.statement: Confirm AUB-P only when one or more clearly defined polyps are documented, generally by hysteroscopy or sonohysterography.
recommendations.context: PALM-COEIN classification of polyps.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.5 | Evaluation of the structure of the endometrial cavity

recommendations.statement: For assessment of a suspected submucous leiomyoma by hysteroscopy or sonohysterography, infuse the distending medium at low pressure; the document states that this distorts the lesion’s natural relationship to the endometrium and myometrium. FIGO recommends hysteroscopy at the lowest pressure needed for assessment when distinguishing Type 2 from Type 3; sonohysterography is considered a suitable, more practical substitute in various clinical circumstances.
recommendations.context: Classification of AUB-LSM.
recommendations.rationale: Distension pressure can alter the apparent anatomical relationships.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.5 | Evaluation of the structure of the endometrial cavity

recommendations.statement: Assess the myometrium primarily with combined TVUS and transabdominal ultrasonography for the primary leiomyoma category; use an appropriate combination of TVUS, contrast sonohysterography, hysteroscopy, and MRI to establish endometrial contact for secondary subclassification.
recommendations.context: Assign LSM if at least one Type 0, 1, 2, or 3 leiomyoma is found; assign Lo if only Types 4, 5, 6, 7, and/or 8 are found.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.6 | Myometrial assessment

recommendations.statement: Evaluate the myometrium for adenomyosis and distinguish leiomyomas from localized adenomyosis or adenomyomas. At present, base AUB-A assignment on imaging findings consistent with the described TVUS criteria or, when available, MRI.
recommendations.context: Myometrial assessment before completion of a FIGO adenomyosis classification system.
recommendations.rationale: The roles of three-dimensional TVUS and sonographic elastography remained under investigation.
recommendations.source_heading: 6.6 | Myometrial assessment

recommendations.statement: Use a structured history and physical examination to begin investigation of chronic AUB. Investigate suspected endocrinopathy when findings suggest an ovulatory disorder, obtain appropriate hematological assessment after a positive coagulopathy screen, and perform a complete blood count in every woman with HMB.
recommendations.context: Initial investigation in the FIGO chronic-AUB algorithm.
recommendations.source_heading: 6 | RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CLINICAL INVESTIGATION

recommendations.statement: If initial assessment indicates increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy, obtain endometrial sampling; if the specimen is inadequate, proceed to hysteroscopic examination and biopsy.
recommendations.context: Uterine assessment in the FIGO chronic-AUB algorithm.
recommendations.source_heading: 6 | RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CLINICAL INVESTIGATION

recommendations.statement: If initial assessment indicates increased risk of a structural abnormality, perform TVUS. If endometrial assessment is suboptimal or suggests a cavity abnormality, proceed to hysteroscopy or contrast hysterosonography; MRI may occasionally be indicated when these are infeasible.
recommendations.context: Uterine assessment in the FIGO chronic-AUB algorithm.
recommendations.source_heading: 6 | RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CLINICAL INVESTIGATION

artifacts.summary: The table identifies revisions to the frequency, regularity, duration, volume, and intermenstrual-bleeding parameters in FIGO System 1.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These parameters support consistent description of bleeding symptoms before their possible causes are assessed.

artifacts.description: The table places the distinction between Types 2 and 3 and between Types 4 and 5 alongside AUB-C, although the accompanying discussion assigns those leiomyoma-type distinctions to AUB-L. The cell is retained in its tabular position.
artifacts.summary: The table records revisions to the PALM-COEIN categories, including changes to leiomyoma subclassification and the reassignment of anticoagulant-associated bleeding to AUB-I.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps prevent use of superseded categories when documenting potential contributors to AUB; its leiomyoma-type row requires attention to the stated inconsistency.

artifacts.title: FIGURE 2 FIGO AUB System 2. PALM-COEIN System for Classification of Causes of AUB in the Reproductive Years.
artifacts.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)
artifacts.description: Step 1: Assess whether a potential cause has visually identifiable structural features → consider the PALM categories: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, or Malignancy and hyperplasia. Step 2: For causes not defined by structural findings → consider the COEI categories: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial disorders, or Iatrogenic causes. Step 3: For an entity not assigned to those categories → use Not otherwise classified. Step 4: Within Leiomyoma, distinguish at least one submucous myoma (LSM) from myomas that do not affect the endometrial cavity (Lo).
artifacts.summary: The classification schematic groups potential AUB causes into structural, nonstructural, and otherwise unclassified categories. It also shows the secondary leiomyoma distinction.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The grouping guides systematic consideration and documentation of possible causes without assuming that every identified lesion produces the bleeding symptoms.

artifacts.title: FIGURE 4 FIGO leiomyoma subclassification system.
artifacts.source_heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)
artifacts.description: Step 1: Determine the lesion’s relationship to the endometrium, myometrium, and serosa. Step 2: For an intracavitary lesion attached to the endometrium by a stalk measuring ≤10% of the mean of three leiomyoma diameters → assign Type 0. If the lesion has an intramural portion of less than 50% of its mean diameter → assign Type 1; if the intramural portion is at least 50% → assign Type 2. Step 3: For a wholly intramural lesion that touches the endometrium → assign Type 3, distinguishing it from Type 2 by hysteroscopy at the lowest intrauterine pressure needed for visualization. Step 4: For a lesion entirely within the myometrium, without reaching the endometrium or serosa → assign Type 4. Step 5: For a subserous lesion, assign Type 5 if at least 50% is intramural, Type 6 if less than 50% is intramural, or Type 7 if it is attached to the serosa by a stalk measuring ≤10% of the mean of three leiomyoma diameters. Step 6: For a transmural lesion → record its endometrial relationship first and serosal relationship second, as in Type 2–5. Step 7: For a leiomyoma without a myometrial relationship, including the specified cervical, ligament, and parasitic lesions → assign Type 8.
artifacts.summary: The schematic defines leiomyoma Types 0 through 8 and the paired notation for transmural lesions according to their anatomical relationships.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The subtype specifies whether a leiomyoma contacts or affects the endometrial cavity and supports consistent characterization of lesions found during AUB assessment.

artifacts.title: FIGURE 5 FIGO AUB System 2 diagnostic matrix.
artifacts.description: Step 1: List each principal FIGO AUB System 2 category and record whether its assessment remains incomplete, is negative, or is positive. Step 2: If a potential cause has not been fully evaluated → mark “?”; if evaluation shows no evidence of it → mark “N”; if it is found → mark the positive box. Step 3: In the illustrated interim assessment of HMB, record the identified subserosal leiomyoma as Lo; leave C and E at “?” while coagulation testing remains outstanding after a positive historical screen. Step 4: When hematological assessment finds no coagulopathy → change C to “N” and mark E as “Y” for the diagnosed primary disorder of endometrial hemostasis.
artifacts.summary: The matrix tracks positive, negative, and unresolved findings across potential AUB causes. Its example shows how classification changes when coagulation results become available.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It distinguishes an incomplete workup from a negative finding and permits documentation of more than one potential contributor.

artifacts.title: FIGURE 6 Investigative algorithms for patients with chronic AUB during the reproductive years.
artifacts.description: Panel A — Step 1: Obtain a structured history and perform a physical examination; choose additional investigations partly according to those findings. Step 2: If findings suggest an ovulatory disorder → assess for endocrinopathy. Step 3: If the coagulopathy screen is positive → undertake appropriate hematological assessment. Step 4: For every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding → perform a complete blood count. Panel B — Step 1: Assess the likelihood of coagulopathy, structural disease, and malignant or premalignant change. Step 2: If these risks are low → AUB-E or -O may be presumed and appropriate treatment offered. Step 3: If risk of endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy is increased → obtain an endometrial sample; if the specimen is inadequate → perform hysteroscopic examination and biopsy. Step 4: If structural abnormality is more likely → perform TVUS. Step 5: If endometrial assessment is inadequate or suggests a cavity abnormality → perform hysteroscopy or contrast hysterosonography. Step 6: If those procedures are impracticable, as may occur in virginal women → MRI may occasionally be indicated.
artifacts.summary: The two-part flowchart links initial clinical assessment to targeted hematological, endocrine, endometrial, and structural investigations.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It guides selection and escalation of investigations according to the suspected cause and the risk of premalignant or malignant disease.

conditions.name: abnormal uterine bleeding
conditions.description: Nongestational bleeding arising from the uterine corpus is characterized using FIGO AUB System 1 before potential causes are assessed with FIGO AUB System 2. More than one condition may contribute to a patient's bleeding, and a structural finding may be incidental.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported prevalence among women of reproductive age is approximately 3%–30%, with higher estimates in adolescents and women in the fifth decade of life and some variation by country. Approximately one third of women are affected at some point. Estimates reach 35% or higher when irregular and intermenstrual bleeding are included alongside heavy menstrual bleeding. Available evidence suggests that as many as half of affected women do not seek care.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Bleeding may differ in duration, volume, frequency or regularity. Its effects range from modest to severe impairment of work productivity and quality of life; pre-existing AUB-related anemia is associated with increased maternal morbidity and mortality during pregnancy.

subtypes.name: chronic nongestational AUB
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bleeding from the uterine corpus that differs from normal in duration, volume, frequency and/or regularity for the majority of the preceding 6 months.

subtypes.name: acute AUB
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An episode of heavy bleeding judged by the clinician to require immediate intervention to limit further blood loss; it may occur with or without preceding chronic AUB.

subtypes.name: heavy menstrual bleeding
subtypes.distinguishing_features: HMB is a symptom rather than a diagnosis. In clinical use, it denotes menstrual blood loss that interferes with physical, social, emotional and/or material quality of life.

subtypes.name: intermenstrual bleeding
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bleeding arising spontaneously between menstrual periods, either cyclically or at random.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize bleeding with FIGO AUB System 1, assess possible contributors and distinguish uterine bleeding from bleeding elsewhere in the genital, urinary or gastrointestinal tract.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment of suspected AUB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A detected abnormality should be assessed for whether it actually contributes to the symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urine or serum assay for the β-subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether bleeding is pregnancy-related.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of reproductive-age women with suspected acute or chronic AUB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Determining pregnancy location or viability lies outside the FIGO AUB systems.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether bleeding comes through the cervical canal rather than from the vagina, vulva, perineum or perianal region.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment of suspected AUB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess iron deficiency.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Acute or chronic AUB, if testing is possible.

diagnostic_workup.test: Hemoglobin and/or hematocrit, preferably a full blood count including platelets
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess associated anemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Acute or chronic AUB; a complete blood count is specified for all women with HMB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record whether each PALM-COEIN cause remains unevaluated, has not been demonstrated or has been identified.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Systematic assessment after a uterine source is confirmed or suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Several categories can apply to one patient; a category left unevaluated must not be treated as excluded.

definitions.description: Structural categories comprising Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, and Malignancy and hyperplasia, generally assessed through imaging and/or histopathology.
Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial disorders and Iatrogenic causes; these categories are not defined by imaging or histopathology.
Not otherwise classified; this category can contain entities with differing capacity to be identified by imaging or histopathology.

staging.additional_rules: The classification permits more than one cause to be recorded. A complete notation can identify the assessment status of every category, while an abbreviated notation records identified categories.

conditions.name: AUB-P
conditions.description: AUB categorized in association with an endometrial or endocervical polyp. Demonstrating a polyp does not by itself establish that it causes the bleeding.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An illustrated patient had intermittent intermenstrual bleeding and an endometrial polyp. The document notes that available evidence suggests a single 1-cm polyp would not account for HMB.

subtypes.name: endometrial polyp
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A polyp within the endometrial cavity.

subtypes.name: endocervical polyp
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A polyp arising in the endocervical region.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for structural abnormalities affecting the uterine cavity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Generally early in the investigation of AUB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A normal examination does not exclude a small polyp.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the cavity and document a clearly defined polyp.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When TVUS suggests a polyp or provides an inadequate assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Documentation of one or more clearly defined polyps supports AUB-P.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inspect the cavity and confirm a clearly defined polyp.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a polyp is suspected or initial cavity assessment is inadequate.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Documentation of one or more clearly defined polyps supports AUB-P.

staging.additional_rules: The P category records a documented polyp; other potential causes may be recorded alongside it.

conditions.name: AUB-A
conditions.description: AUB categorized with imaging findings consistent with adenomyosis. Its relationship with uterine bleeding and reproductive function remains under investigation, and adenomyosis may be asymptomatic.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An illustrated patient had lifelong HMB that was worsening, clots and dysmenorrhea lasting throughout menstruation; imaging also showed features of adenomyosis. That patient additionally had AUB-C.

subtypes.name: adenomyomas
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Localized collections of adenomyosis that may need to be distinguished from leiomyomas.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the myometrium for adenomyosis using the MUSA criteria and distinguish possible adenomyosis from leiomyomas.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Myometrial assessment in AUB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The eight proposed findings are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, hyperechoic islands, fan shaped shadowing, echogenic subendometrial lines and buds, translesional vascularity where present, an irregular junctional zone and an interrupted junctional zone. At least two of these criteria are highly associated with adenomyosis, but there is no consensus on the findings needed for a sufficiently certain diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the presence, location or extent of adenomyosis and help distinguish it from leiomyomas.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When available and needed for myometrial assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document reports that two-dimensional TVUS has sensitivity and specificity similar to MRI for diagnosing adenomyosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assist evaluation of the junctional zone.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When junctional-zone assessment is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its diagnostic role in adenomyosis remains under investigation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigational assessment of adenomyosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its diagnostic role remains under investigation.

staging.additional_rules: AUB-A is assigned on the basis of compatible TVUS findings or, if available, MRI. An adenomyosis subclassification system was still being developed.

conditions.name: AUB-L
conditions.description: AUB categorized in a patient with a leiomyoma. Leiomyomas may be asymptomatic, so their presence does not establish that they contribute to bleeding.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Illustrated presentations include HMB with a posterior Type 2 leiomyoma and irregular bleeding with a posterior Type 6 leiomyoma in a patient whose ovulatory disorder was considered the primary cause.

subtypes.name: LSM
subtypes.distinguishing_features: At least one submucous leiomyoma of Types 0, 1, 2, or 3.

subtypes.name: Lo
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Only leiomyomas of Types 4, 5, 6, 7, and/or 8 are identified.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify leiomyomas and assess uterine and myometrial characteristics.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Primary leiomyoma categorization and imaging-based description.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Any identified leiomyoma permits assignment to the L category; its relationship to the endometrium requires further assessment for subclassification.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the relationship of a leiomyoma to the endometrium and endometrial cavity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a lesion may affect the cavity or its relationship to the endometrium requires clarification.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It can identify submucous lesions and is described as a practical substitute for hysteroscopy in various circumstances when distinguishing Types 2 and 3.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the cavity and distinguish a Type 2 from a Type 3 leiomyoma.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When precise distinction between these types is required.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The distinction is made using the lowest filling pressure that permits visualization of the endometrial cavity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess uterine volume, lesion location, myometrial extent and relationships to the endometrium or serosa; help distinguish leiomyomas from adenomyosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When available and clinically necessary.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: MRI may measure the myometrial extent of submucous leiomyomas better than TVUS, sonohysterography or hysteroscopy, but routine use is not feasible in many healthcare systems.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate uterine size by comparison with a gravid uterus of “X” weeks.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When imaging is unavailable.

definitions.description: An intracavitary leiomyoma attached by a stalk whose diameter is ≤10% of the mean lesion diameter.
A submucous lesion with an intramural portion measuring less than 50% of its mean diameter.
A submucous lesion with an intramural portion measuring at least 50% of its mean diameter.
A wholly intramural lesion that contacts the endometrium without focal distortion of the endometrial cavity.
A lesion wholly within the myometrium, without reaching the endometrial surface or serosa.
A subserous leiomyoma with at least 50% of the lesion intramural and distortion of the serosa.
A subserous leiomyoma with less than 50% of the lesion intramural.
A leiomyoma attached to the serosa by a stalk whose diameter is ≤10% of the mean lesion diameter.
A lesion without a myometrial relationship, including cervical, certain ligament-associated or so-called parasitic leiomyomas.
An example of notation for a transmural lesion: the endometrial relationship is recorded before the serosal relationship.

staging.additional_rules: The minimum imaging-based description includes estimated total uterine volume and the number of leiomyomas (1, 2, 3, 4, or greater than 4). When TVUS or MRI is available, record the location and estimated volume of up to four lesions, their upper-half, lower-half or both vertical location, and their relationship to the endometrium if it is visible. With more than four lesions, record at least the volume of the largest and also document other lesions judged equally or more relevant to clinical decisions. If imaging is unavailable, estimate uterine size clinically.

conditions.name: AUB-M
conditions.description: AUB associated with a malignant or premalignant uterine lesion.
conditions.epidemiology: For women with Lynch Syndrome, the document reports a lifetime endometrial cancer risk of up to 60% and a mean age at diagnosis of 48–50 years; these figures do not describe all patients with AUB-M.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Persistent AUB that is unexplained or inadequately treated warrants endometrial assessment. Obesity is identified as a substantial risk factor for premalignant and malignant endometrial changes, including in women in the third and fourth decades of life.

subtypes.name: endometrial carcinoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A malignant endometrial lesion included in AUB-M.

subtypes.name: leiomyosarcoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A malignant uterine lesion included in AUB-M.

subtypes.name: atypical endometrial hyperplasia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A premalignant lesion included in AUB-M; the document also refers to it as endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia or EIN.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of age, personal risk factors and genetic risk factors
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify patients for whom endometrial sampling is appropriate.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selection of patients with AUB for endometrial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Most cited studies suggest considering sampling above an age threshold, usually 45 years; obesity and a family history of Lynch Syndrome also affect risk.

diagnostic_workup.test: TVUS screening for endometrial echocomplex thickness
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to selection for endometrial sampling.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Risk-based evaluation of AUB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate for premalignant or malignant endometrial change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When risk factors support biopsy, or when AUB remains persistent and unexplained or inadequately treated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An adequate specimen is needed before a patient can be considered at low risk of malignant neoplasia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the cavity and obtain tissue.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If endometrial sampling yields an inadequate specimen; hysteroscopic evaluation is also advised, if possible, with persistent unexplained or inadequately treated AUB.

staging.system: WHO and FIGO classification and staging systems
staging.additional_rules: Malignant and premalignant lesions placed in AUB-M are further characterized with the applicable WHO and FIGO systems; this document does not set out their stage definitions.

conditions.name: AUB-C
conditions.description: AUB associated with a systemic disorder of hemostasis. Bleeding associated with anticoagulant use is instead placed in AUB-I.
conditions.clinical_presentation: HMB may be present from menarche. Historical clues include bleeding after childbirth, surgery or dental work; recurrent bruising or epistaxis; frequent gum bleeding; and a family history of bleeding symptoms.

subtypes.name: vWD Type 1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In an illustrated patient, abnormal measured coagulation parameters were consistent with this disorder.

diagnostic_workup.test: Structured history-based screening instrument for coagulopathies
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen patients with HMB for an underlying hemostatic disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial coagulopathy assessment in patients with excessive menstrual bleeding.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive screen comprises HMB since menarche; one of postpartum hemorrhage, surgical related bleeding or bleeding associated with dental work; or two or more of bruising 1–2 times per month, epistaxis 1–2 times per month, frequent gum bleeding and a family history of bleeding symptoms. The instrument is reported as 90% sensitive in women with HMB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible coagulation disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Following a positive historical screen, potentially with specialist consultation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Positive further testing supports categorization as AUB-C.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible coagulation disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Following a positive historical screen, potentially with specialist consultation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Positive further testing supports categorization as AUB-C.

diagnostic_workup.test: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) and other coagulation measures
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible systemic hemostatic disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Following a positive historical screen.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Positive further testing supports categorization as AUB-C.

staging.additional_rules: Anticoagulant-associated bleeding is assigned to AUB-I rather than AUB-C.

conditions.name: AUB-O
conditions.description: AUB attributed to an ovulatory disorder. Ovulatory disturbances associated with drugs known or suspected to interfere with ovulation are assigned to AUB-I instead.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Bleeding associated with ovulatory disorders is typically irregular in timing and flow and is often interrupted by amenorrhea. Predictable menses every 24–38 days usually, although not invariably, accompany ovulation. An illustrated patient had cycles ranging from 14 to 60 d, bleeding lasting 2 to 11 d, flow ranging from light to heavy and elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone; the ovulatory disorder secondary to hypothyroidism was considered the primary cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize cycle timing, flow and amenorrhea when assessing ovulatory status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected ovulatory disorder in a patient with AUB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Predictable cyclic bleeding suggests, but does not establish, ovulation; irregular bleeding with amenorrhea supports consideration of an ovulatory disorder.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible contributor to an ovulatory disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the initial assessment suggests ovulatory dysfunction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help confirm ovulation in the current cycle.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When ovulatory status is uncertain; measurement is timed to the best estimate of the mid-luteal phase.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess premalignant or malignant endometrial change when otherwise indicated, not determine ovulatory status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Only when indicated for endometrial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Secretory histopathological changes in an appropriately obtained specimen may confirm that ovulation occurred.

staging.additional_rules: Drug-associated interference with ovulation belongs to AUB-I, not AUB-O.

conditions.name: AUB-E
conditions.description: AUB assigned to an endometrial disorder. The document includes primary disorders of endometrial hemostasis and chronic endometritis in this category.
conditions.clinical_presentation: An illustrated assessment attributed HMB to a primary endometrial hemostatic disorder after investigation found no evidence of coagulopathy.

subtypes.name: primary disorder of endometrial hemostasis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as the endometrial explanation in the illustrated patient after hematological assessment did not demonstrate coagulopathy.

subtypes.name: chronic endometritis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: When identified in a patient with AUB, it leads to AUB-E categorization.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish a systemic hemostatic disorder from a primary endometrial hemostatic disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When historical screening raises concern for a coagulation disorder.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In the illustrated diagnostic matrix, testing without evidence of coagulopathy preceded assignment to AUB-E.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible endometrial infection in symptomatic patients.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered in symptomatic patients.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document reports a relationship between endometrial chlamydial infection and AUB; how well a cervical result establishes the presence or absence of endometrial infection is unclear.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible chlamydial infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When infection evaluation is considered.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The correspondence between a cervical specimen and endometrial infection is uncertain.

staging.additional_rules: Identified chronic endometritis is categorized as AUB-E.

conditions.name: AUB-I
conditions.description: AUB associated with an iatrogenic process, including systemic pharmacotherapy, intrauterine systems or devices, anticoagulation, and drugs known or suspected to interfere with ovulation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The document states that rivaroxaban appears to have a greater effect on menstrual bleeding volume than traditional vitamin K antagonists exemplified by warfarin.

subtypes.name: anticoagulant-associated AUB
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bleeding associated with anticoagulant use is classified as AUB-I rather than AUB-C.

subtypes.name: drug-associated ovulatory disorders
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Ovulatory disturbances associated with drugs known or suspected to affect ovulation are classified as AUB-I rather than AUB-O.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a temporal or clinical association of bleeding with systemic medicines or intrauterine systems or devices.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment for iatrogenic contributors to AUB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Agents discussed include estrogens, progestins, androgens, drugs affecting their production or local function, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants, rivaroxaban and warfarin.

staging.additional_rules: This revision assigns anticoagulant-associated AUB and drug-associated ovulatory disturbances to AUB-I.

conditions.name: AUB-N
conditions.description: A category for potential causes of AUB that are uncommon or insufficiently defined and do not fit the other specified categories.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A lower uterine segment or upper cervical niche, also called an isthmocele, is frequently found after cesarean delivery and is sometimes attributed as a cause of AUB.

subtypes.name: arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed among entities accommodated by AUB-N.

subtypes.name: isthmocele
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A lower uterine segment or upper cervical niche associated with previous cesarean delivery and sometimes attributed as a contributor to AUB.

staging.additional_rules: The category is termed Not otherwise classified; its entities may or may not be measurable or definable through imaging or histopathology.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: FIGO first published FIGO AUB System 1, for describing normal and abnormal uterine bleeding symptoms, alongside FIGO AUB System 2, for classifying potential causes through PALM-COEIN, in 2011. The systems were intended to standardize descriptions of bleeding and its possible causes in the reproductive years for research, education, and care, while remaining open to revision. This article reviews, clarifies, and, where appropriate, revises them. The work was largely iterative: the FIGO Menstrual Disorders Committee considered contributions from international epidemiologists, gynecologists, and other experts between 2012 and 2017 through meetings, teleconferences, and other communications. Substantial proposed changes were sometimes decided by anonymous voting using a modified RAND Delphi technique.

document_sections.heading: 1 | INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: AUB affects approximately 3%–30% of women of reproductive age worldwide; estimates differ for reasons that remain unclear, vary somewhat by country, and are higher in adolescence and the fifth decade of life. Approximately one third of women experience AUB at some point. Studies limited to HMB miss other symptoms: including irregular and intermenstrual bleeding raises estimated prevalence to 35% or higher. Available evidence suggests that as many as half of affected women do not seek care even when a healthcare provider is accessible, which may contribute to differences in reported prevalence. Effects range from modest to severe impairment of work and quality of life. Pre-existing AUB-related anemia increases maternal morbidity and mortality in pregnant women. FIGO published two systems and clinical recommendations in 2011 to support research and evidence-based care. Earlier recommendations, initially published in 2007, revised menstrual terminology and normal bleeding parameters. This report updates terminology, definitions, PALM-COEIN category assignments, and leiomyoma subclassification; some changes had appeared previously. Its deliberations included a modified RAND Delphi process at FIGO Menstrual Disorders Committee expert meetings, and it necessarily revisits material from earlier publications so that the report can stand alone. The systems were intended for regular reconsideration as evidence emerged, broadly alongside the triennial FIGO World Congresses. Adenomyosis subclassification is being prepared for preliminary publication followed by validation studies; a polyp system remains in development without a release date. Possible subclassifications for AUB-C, -O, -E, and –I are at very early stages. These FIGO systems address only nongestational AUB: bleeding from elsewhere in the genital tract, urinary tract, or gastrointestinal tract generally can be distinguished through history and physical examination. Earlier recommendations called for abandoning menorrhagia, metrorrhagia, and dysfunctional uterine bleeding because their definitions and international usage were inconsistent.

document_sections.heading: 2 | ACUTE VERSUS CHRONIC NONGESTATIONAL AUB IN THE REPRODUCTIVE YEARS
document_sections.content: FIGO distinguishes acute from chronic nongestational AUB in the reproductive years; the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists endorsed this approach, and its definitions did not change for 2018. Chronic AUB is bleeding from the uterine corpus with abnormal duration, volume, frequency, and/or regularity during the majority of the preceding 6 months. Acute AUB is a heavy-bleeding episode that, in the clinician’s judgment, warrants immediate intervention to reduce or prevent additional blood loss. An acute episode can occur with or without a history of chronic AUB.

document_sections.heading: 3 | FIGO-AUB SYSTEM 1
document_sections.content: FIGO AUB System 1 supplies terminology and definitions for bleeding symptoms. Earlier FIGO work also introduced PALM-COEIN to classify causes in nonpregnant women when no systematic classification existed. PALM groups structural findings identifiable by imaging and/or histopathology: polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyomas, and malignancy or atypical endometrial hyperplasia. COEIN groups causes generally not identifiable by imaging: coagulopathies, ovulatory disorders, primary endometrial disorders, iatrogenic causes, and causes not otherwise classified. Detailed history, examination, and sometimes laboratory tests can suggest or establish these nonstructural causes. Individual categories may need further subdivision by cause and phenotype to improve management and research; leiomyomas were an initial priority. Together, the descriptive systems were designed to give clinicians prompt diagnostic direction while also supporting laboratory investigation and research.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 | Revision of terminologies and definitions of symptoms of abnormal uterine bleeding
document_sections.content: Figure 1 presents the revised FIGO-AUB System 1, and Table 1 summarizes its changes. Menorrhagia, metrorrhagia, oligomenorrhea, and dysfunctional uterine bleeding are no longer used in this system. Bleeding patterns can differ at the adolescent and perimenopausal ends of the reproductive years. Reviews of the system first proposed in 2007 and 2009, slightly revised in 2011, and discussed again at meetings in 2012, 2015, and 2017 led mainly to small refinements informed by clinicians internationally. Regularity is now based on a shortest-to-longest cycle variation of 7–9 days by age rather than up to 20 days: 18–25 years, ≤9 days; 26–41 years, ≤7 days; and 42–45 years, ≤9 days. For practical clinical use, normal cycle-length variation can also be expressed as ±4 days. The revision adds intermenstrual bleeding and uses the 75th percentile for a practical irregular-bleeding threshold so that occasional unusually long or short cycles do not automatically qualify. A correction dated 12 November 2018 changed the frequency label for <24 days to frequent and the irregularity notation to ≥8-10 days. HMB is explicitly a symptom rather than a diagnosis; the adopted National Institute for Health and Care Excellence clinical definition concerns menstrual blood loss excessive enough to interfere with physical, social, emotional, and/or material quality of life. Table 1 also shows that amenorrhea belongs in the frequency category, duration has normal ≤8 d and prolonged >8 d categories, and intermenstrual bleeding is spontaneous bleeding between periods that may occur cyclically or at random.

document_sections.heading: 4 | FIGO AUB SYSTEM 2
document_sections.content: FIGO AUB System 2 classifies potential causes or contributors to AUB in the reproductive years through PALM-COEIN. Its core categories remain largely as originally published; Figure 2 depicts the system, and Table 2 summarizes the revisions.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 | Revision of classification of underlying causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN)
document_sections.content: The nine categories remain Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy and hyperplasia, Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial disorders, Iatrogenic, and Not otherwise classified. PALM comprises four generally discrete structural categories assessable visually with imaging and/or histopathology. COEI comprises four categories not defined by those structural methods. Category N can include entities regardless of whether imaging or histopathology can define them; its name has changed from Not Yet Classified to Not Otherwise Classified because their eventual classification is uncertain. A patient can have several potential contributors, and structural findings such as adenomyosis, leiomyomas, or polyps may be asymptomatic rather than responsible for the presenting bleeding. Since the original system, studies have found similar sensitivity and specificity for two-dimensional transvaginal ultrasonography and MRI in diagnosing adenomyosis, but its relationship with reproductive function and bleeding remains under investigation. There is no consensus on how many or which sonographic findings establish the diagnosis with reasonable certainty. The eight proposed MUSA findings shown in Figure 3 are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, hyperechoic islands, fan-shaped shadowing, echogenic subendometrial lines and buds, translesional vascularity when present, an irregular junctional zone, and an interrupted junctional zone. Three-dimensional ultrasonography may better show the junctional zone, and at least two of the criteria are highly associated with adenomyosis. For FIGO AUB System 2, use of transvaginal ultrasonography-based MUSA criteria is suggested while an international imaging-based subclassification is developed. Leiomyomas have the only ratified subclassification. Type 3 shares endometrial contact with submucous Types 0, 1, and 2, while remaining intramural without focal cavity distortion; applying the system can be difficult, particularly with numerous lesions in a large uterus. Types 0 and 7 have a stalk diameter of 10% or less of the leiomyoma’s mean diameter. Hysteroscopy at the lowest filling pressure that permits cavity visualization is the standard for distinguishing Type 2 from Type 3. Serosal distortion on ultrasonography or MRI distinguishes Type 5 from Type 4. Figure 4 further classifies Type 0 as a stalked intracavitary lesion; Types 1 and 2 as respectively less than 50% and at least 50% intramural; Type 3 as entirely intramural while contacting the endometrium; Type 4 as entirely within the myometrium without reaching endometrium or serosa; Types 5 and 6 as respectively at least 50% and less than 50% intramural; and Type 7 as stalked at the serosa. Transmural lesions are described by endometrial relationship first and serosal relationship second, for example Type 2–5. Type 8 covers lesions without a myometrial relationship, including cervical, unattached round- or broad-ligament, and parasitic lesions. The minimum investigative description of leiomyomas should estimate uterine volume by transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasonography or MRI and record the lesion count as 1, 2, 3, 4, or greater than 4. Without imaging, it should instead estimate uterine size on examination as equivalent to a gravid uterus of “X” weeks. When transvaginal ultrasonography or MRI is available, record the anterior, posterior, left, right, or central position and estimated volume of up to four lesions, as well as whether each lies in the upper half, lower half, or both. With more than four lesions, record at least the largest lesion’s volume and also volumes of any others considered equally or more important to clinical decisions because of location. If the endometrium is visible, describe each documented lesion’s relationship to it using FIGO classification. AUB-M applies when malignant or premalignant uterine lesions accompany AUB, including endometrial carcinoma, leiomyosarcoma, and atypical endometrial hyperplasia, also termed EIN; existing WHO and FIGO systems further classify and stage them. AUB-I covers bleeding associated with systemic pharmacotherapy, intrauterine systems or devices, gonadal steroids, agents affecting steroid production or local effects, and nonsteroidal agents contributing to ovulatory disorders, including dopamine-metabolism-affecting phenothiazines and tricyclic antidepressants. Anticoagulant-associated bleeding has moved from AUB-C to AUB-I; the report states that rivaroxaban appears to affect menstrual bleeding volume more than warfarin. Medication-associated ovulatory disorders likewise no longer belong to AUB-O. AUB-N accommodates uncommon or poorly defined entities, including AVMs and a lower uterine segment or upper cervical niche, or isthmocele, often associated with previous cesarean delivery and sometimes implicated in AUB. Figure 2 also separates patients with at least one submucous leiomyoma, LSM, from those whose leiomyomas do not affect the cavity, Lo. Table 2 summarizes the refined adenomyosis criteria, leiomyoma distinctions, category reassignments, altered ovulatory diagnostic thresholds, and revised AUB-N name.

document_sections.heading: 5 | NOTATION
document_sections.content: Following appropriate investigation, more than one category may represent a potential cause or contributor, so FIGO permits multi-category notation. Although its full form may particularly help specialists and researchers, it can also serve other healthcare providers. Modeled on the comprehensive component-by-component approach of WHO TNM staging, a complete assessment of suspected ovulatory dysfunction and a Type 2 leiomyoma with no other abnormalities can be written AUB P0 A0 L1(SM) M0 - C0 O1 E0 I0 N0; the abbreviated description is AUB-LSM; -O. Because full notation can be cumbersome in clinical practice, a shorter form is available. FIGO encourages a diagnostic matrix that records whether each potential cause remains unassessed, has been excluded by evaluation, or has been found. Figure 5 illustrates a patient with HMB and an Lo subserosal leiomyoma identified by contrast hysterosonography: a positive historical coagulopathy screen leaves relevant categories unresolved until hematological testing finds no coagulopathy, after which a primary endometrial hemostatic disorder is assigned.

document_sections.heading: 6 | RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CLINICAL INVESTIGATION
document_sections.content: AUB can have one or several contributors. Symptoms should first be described with FIGO AUB System 1 before potential causes are investigated under FIGO AUB System 2. A finding may coexist with bleeding without plausibly causing it; available evidence, for example, suggests that a single 1-cm polyp would not account for HMB. Investigation should be as comprehensive as practical for the clinical circumstances and available resources, and each finding’s likely contribution should be assessed. Figure 6 outlines an approach to chronic AUB using history, examination, targeted investigations, and uterine assessment.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 | General assessment
document_sections.content: For acute or chronic genital tract bleeding thought to be AUB in a woman of reproductive age, the clinician should check that it is unrelated to pregnancy and comes from the cervical canal rather than the vagina, vulva, perineum, or perianal region. A urine or serum assay for the β-subunit of hCG can reliably confirm pregnancy; assessing a pregnancy’s site or viability lies outside the FIGO AUB systems. Both acute and chronic AUB warrant evaluation for iron deficiency, preferably through serum ferritin where possible, and associated anemia through hemoglobin and/or hematocrit, preferably a full blood count including platelets. Once a cervical canal or endometrial cavity source is confirmed or suspected, the clinician should assess the PALM-COEIN components systematically.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 | Determination of ovulatory status
document_sections.content: Predictable cycles every 24–38 days usually, though not invariably, accompany ovulation. Ovulatory disorders generally produce irregular bleeding in timing and flow, often interrupted by amenorrhea. When assessment, largely through FIGO AUB System 1, identifies an ovulatory disorder related to AUB, classify it as AUB-O. If ovulation remains uncertain, serum progesterone timed to the estimated mid-luteal phase may confirm ovulation in the current cycle. Endometrial biopsy is not recommended solely to establish ovulatory status. If biopsy is otherwise indicated to investigate premalignant or malignant endometrial change, secretory histopathology may confirm that ovulation occurred.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 | Screening for systemic disorders of hemostasis
document_sections.content: Structured history is a useful screen for coagulopathy. FIGO suggests the instrument in Table 3, which has demonstrated 90% sensitivity in women with HMB; the table identifies combinations of longstanding heavy bleeding, bleeding associated with childbirth, surgery or dental work, bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and family bleeding history as positive screening features. A positive result requires further evaluation, often with a clinician specializing in coagulation disorders, such as a hematologist. Possible tests include von Willebrand factor, Ristocetin cofactor, PTT, and other measures. Positive diagnostic findings support AUB-C. Bleeding associated with anticoagulant treatment is instead classified as AUB-I in this revision.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 | Evaluation of the endometrium
document_sections.content: Endometrial sampling is not necessary for every patient with AUB. Decisions should consider age, personal and genetic risks of premalignant or malignant disease, and TVUS assessment of endometrial echocomplex thickness. Although some studies do not find age independently important, most support considering sampling above a threshold usually set at 45 years. Obesity substantially increases endometrial premalignancy and malignancy risk, including among women in their third and fourth decades. Women with a family history of hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer syndrome, now Lynch Syndrome, have an endometrial cancer lifetime risk of up to 60% and a mean diagnostic age of 48–50 years. Persistent AUB that remains unexplained or inadequately treated requires sampling if possible, irrespective of the clinical guideline, together with hysteroscopic cavity assessment. Sonohysterography is likely a reasonable alternative to hysterography for diagnosing polyps and submucous leiomyomas. An adequate specimen is needed before considering malignancy risk low. Because endometrial chlamydial infection has a reported relationship with AUB, testing symptomatic patients may be prudent. Cervical testing seems reasonable, but how well cervical specimens indicate endometrial infection remains unclear. Identified chronic endometritis belongs in AUB-E.

document_sections.heading: 6.5 | Evaluation of the structure of the endometrial cavity
document_sections.content: Cavity assessment seeks abnormalities potentially contributing to AUB, particularly endometrial or endocervical polyps and submucous leiomyomas. TVUS is an important screening test that should generally be performed early, ideally with equipment and an examiner able to display and interpret endometrial and myometrial detail. Even under ideal conditions it is not 100% sensitive: small lesions and polyps may be missed. Good-quality images without suspicious findings can initially support a presumption of normal cavity structure. Suspected polyps, leiomyomas potentially approaching the cavity, or inadequate imaging warrant more sensitive assessment, generally hysteroscopy and/or gel- or saline-contrast transvaginal ultrasonography, termed sonohysterography; selection depends on available resources. Sonohysterography may be more accessible, whereas office hysteroscopy can allow suspected polyps to be removed during the same encounter. Figure 6 describes initial structured history and examination, assessment for endocrinopathy when ovulatory disorder is suspected, hematological assessment after a positive coagulopathy screen, and a complete blood count for all women with HMB. If initial assessment suggests low coagulopathy, structural, and premalignancy or malignancy risks, AUB-E or -O may be presumed and suitable treatment offered. Elevated endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy risk calls for sampling; an inadequate specimen calls for hysteroscopy and biopsy. Greater structural risk calls for TVUS, followed by hysteroscopy or contrast hysterosonography if endometrial assessment is inadequate or a cavity lesion is suspected. MRI may occasionally be indicated if those procedures are infeasible. Some services, notably the UK National Health Service, emphasize evaluating and managing HMB at the first consultation through history, examination, TVUS, and hysteroscopy when indicated; FIGO AUB System 1 describes symptoms before FIGO AUB System 2 categorizes investigated findings. Vaginal access may be difficult or impossible, especially in adolescents and virginal women, making TVUS, contrast sonohysterography, or office hysteroscopy infeasible; MRI has a role, or hysteroscopy with indicated biopsies under appropriate anesthesia may be preferable. An AUB-P designation requires documentation of clearly defined polyps, generally through hysteroscopy or sonohysterography. Either method usually permits identification of submucous leiomyomas as AUB-LSM. Distending medium should be infused at low pressure when assessing the lesion’s relationship to the endometrium and myometrium. FIGO recommends hysteroscopy at the lowest pressure adequate for assessment to distinguish Type 2 from Type 3; sonohysterography is considered an appropriate, more practical substitute in various circumstances. Figure 7 provides illustrative diagnostic-matrix cases: a patient with HMB lasting 10 d had a posterior Type 2 leiomyoma measuring 1.85 by 1.49 cm on contrast sonohysterography and otherwise negative investigations, yielding AUB-LSM. Another patient’s cycles ranged from 14 to 60 d, bleeding lasted 2 to 11 d, and flow ranged from light to heavy; TVUS found a posterior Type 6 leiomyoma and thyroid-stimulating hormone was elevated, yielding AUB-Lo; -O, with hypothyroidism-related ovulatory dysfunction judged the primary cause. A patient with otherwise normal menstrual parameters and intermittent intermenstrual bleeding had an endometrial polyp and Type 5 leiomyoma; the polyp was considered the primary cause of AUB-P; -Lo. A patient with lifelong HMB that had worsened, clots, worsening dysmenorrhea throughout menstruation, easy bruising, and bleeding during toothbrushing had predictable 33 d cycles; TVUS showed a globular uterus, posterior asymmetrical myometrial thickening, and fan-shaped shadowing, while abnormal coagulation results were consistent with vWD Type 1, yielding AUB-A, -C.

document_sections.heading: 6.6 | Myometrial assessment
document_sections.content: Primary leiomyoma categorization relies mainly on combined TVUS and transabdominal ultrasonography; any identified leiomyoma warrants an L assignment. Secondary subclassification establishes whether a leiomyoma contacts the endometrium through an appropriate combination of TVUS, contrast sonohysterography, hysteroscopy, and MRI. One or more submucous Types 0, 1, 2, or 3 gives LSM; exclusively Types 4, 5, 6, 7, and/or 8 gives Lo. Tertiary classification requires defining relationships with endometrium, cavity, myometrium, and serosa. Imaging is needed particularly for lesions of Types 3 and higher that do not distort the cavity; MRI can be more accurate than ultrasonography for this purpose. Assess the myometrium for adenomyosis and distinguish leiomyomas from localized adenomyosis or adenomyomas. Pending a FIGO adenomyosis classification, AUB-A is best assigned from consistent TVUS findings or, where available, MRI. The diagnostic roles of three-dimensional TVUS and sonographic elastography remain under investigation. MRI may be necessary to distinguish leiomyomas from adenomyosis and may measure the myometrial extent of submucous leiomyomas better than TVUS, sonohysterography, or hysteroscopy. Routine reliance on MRI is nevertheless impractical in many healthcare systems, particularly in low-resource countries, because access may be limited or absent.

document_sections.heading: 7 | DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: AUB in reproductive-age women can manifest numerous disorders or pathological entities. FIGO AUB System 1 describes symptoms, while FIGO AUB System 2 classifies possible causes; together they aim to support basic and clinical research and consistent, rational medical and surgical care. The revisions seek to improve their usefulness in research, education, and practice. Clinicians, educators, and investigators are encouraged to use the diagnostic matrix for chronic AUB and for acute AUB once the patient is stabilized. Development and revision involved participants from six continents and considered whether the investigations required for PALM-COEIN categorization are practical. Routine MRI characterization of structural uterine lesions is not feasible and is not mandatory for chronic AUB assessment. This does not preclude MRI when it is considered necessary and available to establish leiomyoma type or the presence, absence, location, or extent of adenomyosis.

document_sections.heading: 8 | CONCLUSION
document_sections.content: The article brings together changes to both FIGO AUB systems following 6 years of analysis, discussion, and debate since the original publication. It integrates refined symptom terminology and definitions from System 1 with the PALM-COEIN classification of potential causes in System 2.
